description: We are Team Apollo-14, participating in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge in São Paulo. Our focus is the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. We are interested in space exploration, astronomy, software development, data analysis, visualization, and artificial intelligence. We are looking for motivated teammates who enjoy solving problems, sharing ideas, and building innovative solutions. Developers, data analysts, researchers, designers, and science enthusiasts are welcome.
summary:
Planet X is a web app for exploring real SPHEREx observations from NASA’s Infrared Science Archive. It provides a searchable interface for entering sky coordinates, choosing a field of view, and selecting challenge target presets. The app is built with Next.js, with its API routes and frontend deployed together.

The project addresses the challenge of investigating objects that may change over time by creating a foundation for comparing observations and examining possible motion or variability. It emphasizes traceable data, coordinate provenance, and clear communication of uncertainty so that users can distinguish evidence from assumptions.

This work matters because repeated observations can help researchers study changing sources and identify candidates for further investigation. Planet X is an initial prototype: live archive search, temporal analysis, and motion or variability detection are planned, but are not yet implemented.
details:
Planet X is a web application for exploring NASA’s SPHEREx observations. Users enter sky coordinates or choose a target preset, set a field diameter, and select the DR1 and/or QR3 data collection. The app sends the search to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) SIA2 service and presents returned observation metadata and links to archive products. It reports when there is no coverage or when the archive cannot be reached.

The project makes SPHEREx data easier to explore and provides a starting point for studying how astronomical sources change over time. Its intended impact is to help researchers and curious users find relevant observations while keeping the data’s source and coordinate assumptions visible. The current version searches archive metadata; temporal viewing, FITS analysis, and motion or variability detection are future work.

We built the app with TypeScript, React, and Next.js, including server-side API routes for archive queries. Development focused on clear coordinate validation, traceable archive links, handling incomplete or unavailable results, and avoiding unsupported scientific claims. We also considered field size, sky coverage, and the risk of treating an unknown coordinate epoch as known.
